title: The Cheap Alternative to the Japan Rail Pass: Riding the Old Tokaido Line Slowly
description: JR sells a seasonal ticket giving three consecutive days of unlimited travel on local and rapid trains for under ¥8,000 — no bullet trains, no reservations, and no requirement to be a tourist. Here is how it works, the Tokyo-to-Shizuoka route worth using it on, and where to stay beside each station.
intro: Since the Japan Rail Pass rose sharply in price, a lot of visitors have worked out that it no longer pays for their trip — and then assumed the only alternative is buying individual bullet train tickets. There is a third option that almost no guide written for foreigners mentions, because it is aimed at the domestic market: JR sells seasonal passes giving three or five consecutive days of unlimited travel on local and rapid trains, for less than the price of one Tokyo–Kyoto bullet train ticket. Anyone can buy one, including you. The catch is the obvious one — no shinkansen, no limited express, no reserved seats — which turns a 100-minute journey into most of a day. That is either a serious drawback or the entire point, depending on the trip you want. This guide covers how these passes work and when they are sold, then sets out the route they suit best: the old Tokaido line west from Tokyo, through Odawara, Atami and Shizuoka, stopping at hot spring towns and eating your way along the coast. Every hotel below is chosen for one reason above all — how close it is to the station.
listHeading: Where to stay along the Tokaido line, station by station

buyingGuide.title: This is not the Japan Rail Pass — know the difference
buyingGuide.body: The Japan Rail Pass is the well-known one: expensive, sold mainly to foreign tourists, and valid on most shinkansen. What this guide is about is a different product entirely, sold seasonally for the domestic market. It covers unlimited travel on JR local and rapid trains only — no shinkansen, no limited express, no reserved or green-car seats — for a set number of consecutive days, at a price of roughly ¥8,000 for three days. Unlike the Japan Rail Pass it carries no residency or visa restriction, so overseas visitors can buy it. It also cannot be bought outside Japan or online from abroad; you buy it at a JR ticket office once you are here.

buyingGuide.title: The passes are seasonal — check what is on sale for your dates
buyingGuide.body: These tickets are not available year-round. The best known is the Seishun 18 Kippu, sold for periods covering spring, summer and winter; an autumn equivalent covers a short window in October. Each has its own sale period, validity period, price and rules, and JR adjusts them from time to time — the Seishun 18 was significantly reworked in recent years, so older guides are unreliable. The autumn ticket has typically been priced around ¥7,850 for three consecutive days, sold from mid-September for use in the first half of October, but treat every one of those numbers as something to verify. Check the current terms on JR's own site before planning around one.

buyingGuide.title: Work out honestly whether the slow train suits your trip
buyingGuide.body: Tokyo to Shizuoka takes roughly an hour by shinkansen and around three and a half to four hours by local trains with several changes. If your itinerary is tight, this pass is a false economy — you are paying with the scarcest thing you have. It makes sense in three situations: you have weeks rather than days in Japan; you actively want to see the country between the cities rather than pass under it in a tunnel; or you are travelling on a tight budget and time is the resource you have most of. Decide which of those describes you before buying, because there is no upgrade path once you are on the train.

buyingGuide.title: Practical realities of local trains
buyingGuide.body: There are no reserved seats, so on busy stretches you stand — avoid commuter hours around the big cities, and you will usually get a seat. Trains are shorter and less frequent the further you get from Tokyo, so plan connections in advance rather than turning up and hoping; a journey planner is essential, and a missed connection can cost an hour. Not every train has a toilet. Buy food and drink at stations rather than expecting a trolley service. The pass covers consecutive days, so the clock runs whether you travel or not — do not buy a three-day pass for a trip with a rest day in the middle.

buyingGuide.title: Send your luggage ahead — local trains have nowhere to put it
buyingGuide.body: This is the detail that separates a good version of this trip from a miserable one. Shinkansen have luggage space; local commuter trains have overhead racks designed for a briefcase, and you will be changing trains several times with people getting on and off around you. Use one of Japan's luggage forwarding services to send your main suitcase ahead to a later hotel or the airport, and travel with a small bag. It is inexpensive, hotels handle it for you at reception, and it typically takes a day, so send it the morning before you need it.

buyingGuide.title: Choose hotels by their distance from the station, not their rating
buyingGuide.body: On a trip built around trains, ten minutes' walk with a bag at the end of a long day matters more than an extra half point of review score. Stations along this route have hotels attached to or directly beside them — a genuine luxury when you are arriving and departing by train daily. It also lets you drop your bag on arrival and explore unencumbered, and leave promptly the next morning. The list below is ordered along the route from east to west rather than by quality, so you can read it as an itinerary: night one at Odawara or Atami, night two at Shizuoka, with an optional extension west to Lake Hamana.

places.name: Tenseien Odawara Station Annex
places.japaneseName: 天成園 小田原駅 別館
places.area: Odawara · directly connected to the station, about 90 minutes from Tokyo
places.description: The first natural stop heading west, and the one to pick if you want to break the journey early rather than push on. Odawara is a castle town at the entrance to the Hakone region, known for its fish cakes and its harbour food, and this hotel sits inside the Minaka Odawara complex directly connected to the station — you reach it without going outside, which matters in October rain. The top floor has an open-air hot spring bath looking over the town, which is a good deal more than a station hotel normally offers. Rated around 4.2 out of 5 across more than 1,800 reviews. Note the trade: this is a modern complex rather than a traditional inn, so book it for convenience, not atmosphere.
pros: Directly connected to Odawara Station — no walk with luggage
Rooftop open-air hot spring bath with a view over the town
Odawara Castle and the harbour food streets are close by
cons: A modern station complex rather than a traditional inn
Bathing hours and access conditions vary — confirm when booking

places.name: Hotel Kanichi, Atami Onsen
places.japaneseName: 熱海温泉 お部屋食と源泉かけ流しの宿 ホテル貫一
places.area: Atami · night one, the classic hot spring stop on this line
places.description: The best first night on the route if you want the traditional experience rather than a station hotel. Atami is a hot spring town built up a steep bay about twenty minutes beyond Odawara, and this inn's two selling points are exactly what you want after a day of changing trains: hot spring water piped straight from the source without recirculation, and dinner served in your own room rather than a dining hall. For overseas visitors that second point quietly solves a lot — no working out where to sit, no set dinner time in a room full of strangers, and you can eat in a yukata with the door shut. Rated around 4.4 out of 5 across more than 1,800 reviews. Check the walking distance from the station when booking.
pros: Dinner served in your own room — no communal dining hall
Hot spring water direct from the source, not recirculated
cons: Walking distance from the station varies — confirm before booking
Atami is busy at weekends and during Japanese holidays

places.name: KKR Hotel Atami
places.japaneseName: 熱海温泉 KKRホテル熱海
places.area: Atami · the budget alternative for night one, sea views
places.description: The cheaper way to spend night one in Atami. It stands on high ground near the station with rooms and a communal hot spring bath looking out over Sagami Bay, and it is run as a public-service hotel, which in Japan generally means plain but well-kept rooms at prices below the commercial equivalent. That suits this trip: if the point of the pass is to travel cheaply, spending the saving on a sea view rather than on a ryokan dinner is a reasonable trade. Rated around 4.2 out of 5. Two things to check — the view depends on which room type you book, and the hillside position means the walk from the station is uphill, which matters with a bag.
pros: Sea views over Sagami Bay from rooms and the communal bath
Noticeably cheaper than the ryokan option for the same night
Near the station, with a steady 4.2/5 rating
cons: The view depends entirely on the room type you book
Uphill walk from the station — awkward with luggage

places.name: Hotel Associa Shizuoka
places.area: Shizuoka · night two, directly connected to the station
places.description: The obvious base for night two, and the most convenient hotel on this route. It connects directly to Shizuoka Station, so you step off the train and you are effectively there — worth a great deal on a trip where you arrive and leave by train every day. Shizuoka is the reason to stop here: green tea country, an excellent local seafood market at nearby Shimizu, the pine grove at Miho-no-Matsubara with its view of Mount Fuji across the bay, and oden served in a style particular to the city. Drop your bag and go. Rated around 4.4 out of 5 across more than 3,400 reviews. It is a city hotel, so there is no hot spring — the compensation is that you are a lift ride from the platform.
pros: Directly connected to Shizuoka Station — the easiest arrival on the route
Good base for Shimizu, Miho-no-Matsubara and the city's oden
cons: A city hotel with no hot spring or communal bath
Rates rise during Japanese holiday periods

places.name: Shizutetsu Hotel Prezio Shizuoka Ekiminami
places.japaneseName: 静鉄ホテルプレジオ 静岡駅南
places.area: Shizuoka · the value option for night two, walking distance from the station
places.description: The cheaper choice for night two, and the one that fits the spirit of the trip. It is a short walk from Shizuoka Station on the south side, with clean, functional rooms and a breakfast that reviewers consistently single out — the sort of well-run Japanese business hotel that has no international equivalent at the price. Rated around 4.3 out of 5 across more than 3,200 reviews. If you are travelling on local trains to save money, this is where the logic holds: the room costs a fraction of the station-connected option, and the difference covers a good deal of eating in a city known for its food. The walk is short but not zero, so check the exact distance if you are carrying everything.
pros: Well below the station-connected option, with a strong breakfast reputation
cons: No hot spring or communal bath — a straightforward business hotel
A short walk rather than direct access; check the distance

places.name: Tokiwasure Kaikatei, Lake Hamana
places.japaneseName: 浜名湖かんざんじ温泉 時わすれ 開華亭
places.area: Lake Hamana, Kanzanji Onsen · if you extend a night further west
places.description: The reason to add a third night and keep going west. Lake Hamana is a large brackish lagoon near Hamamatsu, and the country's best-known area for freshwater eel — grilled unagi here is a destination dish rather than a menu item, and the Kanzanji hot spring sits on the lake shore. This inn faces the water, keeps to a traditional style, and makes a fitting end to a slow train trip. Rated around 4.1 out of 5. Be clear about the trade-off before booking: this is the one property on the list that is not near a station. You reach it by bus from Hamamatsu, so check the timetable and whether the inn offers a pickup, and do not plan a tight connection around it.
pros: Lakeside hot spring in Japan's best-known area for grilled eel
Traditional style — a fitting end to a slow rail trip
Turns the route into a comfortable three or four nights
cons: The only stop here that is not near a station — bus from Hamamatsu
Check bus times and pickup availability before committing

faq.question: Can foreign visitors buy these seasonal passes?
faq.answer: Yes. Unlike the Japan Rail Pass, which is restricted to visitors on a temporary visitor status, the seasonal local-train passes carry no residency or nationality condition — they are domestic products that anyone can buy. The limitation is where: you cannot buy them from outside Japan or through the overseas booking channels that sell the Japan Rail Pass. You buy one at a JR ticket office or, in some cases, a ticket machine, once you have arrived. Bring your passport for identification if asked, though it is not normally required in the way it is for the Japan Rail Pass.

faq.question: How is this different from the Japan Rail Pass?
faq.answer: Almost completely. The Japan Rail Pass is expensive, sold mainly to tourists, valid for seven days or more, and covers most shinkansen — it is designed for covering long distances quickly. These seasonal passes cost a fraction as much, run for three or five consecutive days, and are valid only on local and rapid trains with unreserved seating. No shinkansen, no limited express. They suit slow travel over short-to-medium distances, not a Tokyo–Hiroshima dash. Since the Japan Rail Pass increased sharply in price, working out which one actually fits your itinerary is worth the ten minutes it takes.

faq.question: How long does Tokyo to Shizuoka actually take on local trains?
faq.answer: Roughly three and a half to four hours, with several changes, against about an hour by shinkansen. That gap is the whole decision. If you are in Japan for ten days and want to see as much as possible, this is the wrong ticket. If you have several weeks, or you specifically want to watch the coast go past and stop in towns most visitors skip, it is the right one. The route in this guide is designed around that reality: short hops with a stop each night, rather than one long day of riding.

faq.question: Will I get a seat?
faq.answer: Usually, if you avoid commuter hours. There are no reserved seats on these trains, so seating is first-come. The stretches around Tokyo and Yokohama are crowded during the morning and evening rush and you may stand; further west the trains empty out and seats are easy. Travelling between about 10am and 4pm makes a substantial difference. Trains also become shorter and less frequent the further you go, so check connection times in advance — a missed connection in a rural section can mean an hour on the platform.

faq.question: What do I do with my suitcase?
faq.answer: Send it ahead. Local trains have no luggage storage comparable to the shinkansen, and you will be changing trains repeatedly. Japan's luggage forwarding services will take a case from one hotel to another, or to an airport, usually overnight and for a modest fee; hotel reception desks arrange it as a matter of routine. Travel with an overnight bag and let the case meet you further down the line. Station coin lockers are a fallback but fill up, and the large ones go first.

faq.question: Which season are these passes available in?
faq.answer: They are sold in seasonal blocks rather than year-round. The long-running Seishun 18 Kippu covers periods in spring, summer and winter, and a separate autumn ticket covers a short window in October. Each has its own sale dates, validity dates, price and conditions, and JR has changed the rules more than once in recent years, so guides written even a couple of years ago can be wrong. Before building a trip around one, check JR's current terms for the exact period you are travelling — including whether the days must be consecutive, which they generally are.
